blocks.text: If you’ve made it this far, it’s time to put all the pieces together and find out who murdered Joseph Maroun.

But before we reveal the murderer, let’s go back to the beginning and examine what actually happened during Joseph’s final week in Lebanon. Because throughout this investigation, you’ve been presented with numerous testimonies, photographs, receipts, and documents. Some of them appeared completely ordinary, while others made certain family members look incredibly suspicious. But as you’re about to discover, not every suspicious action was connected to Joseph’s murder, and some of the most important clues were hidden in the smallest details.
Monday, September 14 – Wednesday, September 16

Joseph and his mother, Tina, arrived in Lebanon on Monday, September 14, 2026. During their stay in Beirut, they were hosted by Joseph’s aunt, France Jabbour. The following day, Joseph traveled to Miye w Miye to deal with legal matters concerning a property that had recently been transferred into his name.

On Wednesday, Joseph returned to Beirut. That same day, he paid France’s electricity bill, which apparently caused an argument between them. According to France’s interview, she was upset because Joseph was her guest, and she believed it was her responsibility to take care of him, not the other way around. The argument was supposedly resolved quickly, and the two went grocery shopping at Spinneys later that day.

At first glance, none of this seems particularly important. After all, a disagreement over an electricity bill hardly seems like a motive for murder, and there was nothing particularly suspicious about a trip to the supermarket.
But remember these details. We’ll come back to them later.
For now, let’s move on to Thursday.
Thursday, September 17

On Thursday, Joseph and Doris went hiking together in the Cedars. According to Doris’s statement, the two spent the day together, and the photograph taken during their hike confirms that her account of the timeline was accurate. There were no apparent inconsistencies in her story, and nothing suggested that she had lied about their outing.
However, that photograph wasn’t included in the evidence merely to confirm when and where they went hiking. There’s another important detail hidden in that picture, and we’ll come back to it shortly.

Now, let’s talk about Doris’s financial situation. As you may have noticed from the mortgage documents, Doris was experiencing serious financial difficulties. She had fallen behind on her payments and was under considerable financial pressure. She needed money, and she needed it rather urgently.

Then, following Joseph’s death, Doris inherited a share of his property. And on September 25, just five days after his death, she sold her inherited shares to someone. Rather convenient timing, wouldn’t you say? A woman struggling financially suddenly inherits a valuable asset, sells it almost immediately, and obtains the money she desperately needs.
This certainly raises some questions. Did Doris murder Joseph to obtain that inheritance, or did she simply benefit from an unexpected opportunity following his death?
Keep that question in mind as we continue.
Friday, September 18
Now, moving on to Friday, and here’s where I want you to pay particularly close attention.

That morning, France hosted a family brunch, and everyone was present. All the testimonies agree on this, and the photographs taken that day support their statements. There are no significant contradictions concerning who attended or what happened during the gathering.
But what I want you to focus on is what happened AFTER the brunch.

Joseph and Perla spent the afternoon together. They visited a museum, went bowling, played billiards, and eventually stopped by the casino. Nothing particularly unusual about that, right? They were simply spending time together and enjoying their day.
Well, let’s take a closer look at the casino.

During her interview, Perla claimed that she and Joseph didn’t stay there for long. In fact, to use her exact words, “We left before it got dark.” She also claimed that she was with Joseph “the entire evening.”

But now, take another look at the casino account statement. You’ll notice that the account is registered under Perla’s name, and according to the records, gambling activity took place between 7:24 p.m. and 8:16 p.m. That’s already after dark. So, something doesn’t add up. If Perla and Joseph left the casino before dark, why was there gambling activity on her account later that evening?

To answer that question, let’s examine the screenshot of their conversation. At 7:58 p.m., Joseph sent Perla a message asking, “Where are you?” Think about that for a moment. If Perla was with Joseph the entire evening, as she claimed, why would he need to ask where she was?
Because she wasn’t with him.
She lied.
And if you remember her police interview, the officer had already given you a clue when he told her, “Lying to the police makes you suspicious.”

Here’s what actually happened. After spending the afternoon together, Perla and Joseph left the casino. But later that evening, Perla decided to return on her own, without telling anyone. She wanted to try her luck at gambling, hoping she might win some money and perhaps even help her mother with her financial difficulties.

Unfortunately, things didn’t go as planned. She started losing, and instead of stopping, she convinced herself that if she kept playing, she could eventually win back everything she had lost. But the more she played, the more money she lost. By the end of the evening, Perla had lost a total of $8,980.

At 8:27 p.m., overwhelmed and panicking, she called Joseph and confessed what had happened. Joseph was understandably furious and insisted that she tell her mother. In fact, his message made his position perfectly clear: “Tell your mom or I will.”

Now, imagine Perla’s situation. She had just lost almost $9,000, she had no idea how she was going to recover the money, and Joseph was threatening to expose everything to her mother. She was terrified of what would happen if her family discovered what she had done.
But here’s the question: Could Perla have gone so far as to murder Joseph to prevent him from exposing her secret?
After all, remember the speeding ticket?
Take another look at the vehicle captured by the speed camera. A grey Kia Rio. Now, go back to the suspect profiles. Who drives a grey Kia Rio? That’s right. Perla.

On Saturday, September 19, just one day before Joseph’s body was discovered, Perla’s car was caught speeding on the R-05 highway. And if you look at the map provided in the evidence, you’ll notice something interesting: the R-05 is the road connecting Beirut to Miye w Miye, the very place where Joseph was found dead the following morning.

evidence.caption: Map of locations and the R-05

blocks.text: Was Perla rushing to Miye w Miye to confront Joseph? Was she afraid that he would expose her gambling losses to her mother? Did she decide to silence him before he had the opportunity to tell anyone? And could that confrontation have ended in murder?
Well, before we answer those questions, there’s something else we need to discuss.
The theft.
Remember how Joseph mentioned that something had been stolen from him? But what exactly was missing? Believe it or not, the answer has been right in front of you throughout the entire investigation.

Think back to all the photographs of Joseph. The photograph published in the newspaper, the photograph taken during his hike with Doris, and even the pictures from Friday’s family brunch. What do all these photographs have in common?
Joseph was wearing a watch.

Every single time Joseph appeared in a photograph, he had a watch on his wrist. And this is precisely why those photographs were included in the evidence. They weren’t simply there to illustrate the events of his visit or confirm everyone’s statements. They were also meant to establish that Joseph consistently wore the same watch.

Now, take another look at the photograph of Joseph’s personal belongings collected by the police following his death. His wallet was there, his phone was there, his keys were there, and his other personal belongings had been carefully gathered and placed into evidence bags.
But something was missing.
The watch.

The very same watch Joseph had been wearing throughout his visit was nowhere to be found among the belongings collected by the police. Now, the absence of a watch alone wouldn’t necessarily prove that someone had stolen it. But when you combine that detail with Joseph’s statement that something had been taken from him, the pieces begin to fall into place.
Someone had stolen Joseph’s watch. But who?

Let’s return to Perla. We already know that she had lost nearly $9,000 at the casino and was desperate to recover the money. We also know that she had spent Friday afternoon with Joseph, giving her an opportunity to take the watch. And most importantly, we know that Joseph was threatening to expose her secret to her mother.

Now, remember that speeding ticket from Saturday? There’s one detail about the R-05 highway that we haven’t discussed yet. Yes, it leads from Beirut toward Miye w Miye, but if you look carefully at the map, you’ll notice that the casino is located along that very same route.

evidence.caption: Map of locations and the R-05

blocks.text: So, what if Perla wasn’t rushing toward Joseph’s house at all? What if she was rushing toward the casino?

Here’s what actually happened. Desperate to recover the money she had lost, Perla stole Joseph’s valuable watch, intending to use it to cover her gambling debt. The following day, she rushed toward the casino to deal with her financial situation, driving so fast that she received a speeding ticket.
Her destination wasn’t Joseph’s house in Miye w Miye. It was the casino.

And there was another reason Perla was so desperate to keep everything hidden. She was preparing to become a judge, and she knew that being involved in a gambling scandal could seriously damage her reputation and jeopardize her chances of entering the judiciary. Imagine what would happen to her ambitions if it became known that she had engaged in gambling, an activity prohibited by law.

That explains why she lied about her movements, concealed her gambling activity, and was terrified of Joseph exposing her. She wasn’t simply afraid of disappointing her mother. She was afraid of destroying the future she had been working toward.
Perla was hiding a crime. But it wasn’t murder.
She had stolen Joseph’s watch, and although her actions made her an obvious suspect, they did not make her Joseph’s killer.
Saturday, September 19 – The Night of the Murder
Let’s move on to Saturday, the day before Joseph’s body was discovered.

Joseph and his mother, Tina, returned to Miye w Miye, where they went out for dinner at Saniour. They shared a meal, yet only Joseph was poisoned. Could the poisoning have happened at the restaurant? Possibly. However, the fact that Tina ate with him and remained unharmed raises questions about whether dinner was really the source of the poisoning.

As for Tina herself, there is no evidence establishing a motive for her to murder her own son. Nothing in her testimony or the documents suggests that she wanted Joseph dead. Although we cannot eliminate someone simply because she is a mother, there is no convincing evidence pointing toward Tina as the murderer.
Now, let’s talk about Bernard.

Bernard was certainly one of our most suspicious characters. As a farmer, he regularly handled agricultural chemicals, some of which could potentially be dangerous. In fact, if you look at the receipt dated Thursday, September 17, you’ll notice that he purchased several agricultural products just two days before Joseph’s death. And let’s not forget the photograph of his gardening shed, where several chemical products were stored. Quite suspicious, wouldn’t you say?

But that’s not all. Throughout Joseph’s visit to Lebanon, Bernard had repeatedly expressed his frustration over the property in Miye w Miye. Then, on Saturday evening, he visited Joseph’s house, and the two got into yet another heated argument. According to Tina, the argument eventually ended, Bernard left, and Joseph remained at home.

So, let’s put everything together. Bernard had a possible motive, access to potentially dangerous substances, and a heated confrontation with Joseph shortly before his death. He was also among the last people known to have seen Joseph alive. But does that necessarily mean Bernard murdered him?

Not quite. Remember, there was a witness to their argument: Tina. She was present when Bernard confronted Joseph, heard parts of their conversation, and confirmed that Bernard eventually left the house. This is an important detail because Bernard could hardly have attacked Joseph or openly administered a poisonous substance without risking Tina noticing something suspicious. And according to her testimony, she witnessed nothing of the sort.
Bernard’s anger, his access to potentially dangerous substances, and his presence at the house certainly made him suspicious, but suspicion alone is not enough to establish guilt.
And this is where we need to focus on something far more important. If Bernard wasn’t responsible for Joseph’s death, then perhaps something happened AFTER he left.
So, what exactly happened after Bernard left the house?

According to Tina’s testimony, Joseph was furious following the argument. He had had enough for one day and didn’t want to go anywhere or speak to anyone. Tina was supposed to visit her brother-in-law that evening, so she asked Joseph whether he wanted to accompany her. He refused, explaining that he preferred to stay home, watch a movie, and make himself an argileh.
Now, I want you to pay very close attention to that last detail. Joseph wanted to make himself an argileh.

Remember the photograph taken at the crime scene? If you look closely, you’ll notice that an argileh was sitting there, exactly as Tina had described. And what did the autopsy establish? Joseph died from poisoning. So, what if the poisoning had nothing to do with the restaurant? What if Bernard never poisoned Joseph during their argument? What if the substance responsible for Joseph’s death was already inside his home, waiting to be used?

Think about it. Joseph stayed home that evening, watched a movie, and prepared his argileh. The argileh was later found at the crime scene, and the autopsy confirmed that he had been poisoned. Could the tobacco have been contaminated?

If that is what happened, then the entire investigation takes a different direction. Instead of focusing exclusively on the people who saw Joseph on Saturday evening, we need to consider someone who had access to his belongings BEFORE Saturday. Someone who didn’t necessarily need to be anywhere near Miye w Miye on the night of his death.
And that brings us back to something I asked you to remember at the very beginning of this investigation.
Wednesday, September 16.

Remember the disagreement between France and Joseph over the electricity bill? According to France’s testimony, she was upset because Joseph had paid the bill himself. She explained that Joseph was her guest, and she believed it was her responsibility to take care of him, not the other way around. A perfectly reasonable explanation, at least at first glance.
But now, I want you to take another look at the Spinneys receipt from that same Wednesday. More specifically, look at the payment information. Who paid for the groceries?
That’s right. Joseph Maroun.
France had supposedly been upset that Joseph paid her electricity bill, yet later that very same day, she allowed him to pay for the groceries. Isn’t that a little strange? Something doesn’t add up.

Perhaps France wasn’t being entirely truthful about the argument the neighbor overheard that Wednesday. Perhaps the electricity bill was simply a convenient explanation for a disagreement that had actually been about something else.

But the payment information isn’t the most important detail on that receipt. There is something else I want you to notice. Take another look at the list of items purchased that day. Among all the ordinary groceries, there is one particular item that should immediately catch your attention.
Argileh tobacco.
Yes, tobacco. The very same thing Joseph intended to use on Saturday evening, shortly before his death. And who was with Joseph when that tobacco was purchased? France.
Now, here is the detail that changes everything, and it is something you have known since the very beginning of the investigation: Joseph and Tina were staying at France’s house in Beirut.

That means France wasn’t simply present when the tobacco was purchased. She also had access to Joseph’s belongings throughout his stay. She didn’t need to travel to Miye w Miye on Saturday evening, confront Joseph, or even be anywhere near him when he died. She had an opportunity to interfere with his belongings days before he returned to his house.

While everyone was concentrating on the people who had seen Joseph shortly before his death, we had overlooked someone who had access to his belongings long before that evening. Someone who could have prepared everything in advance, without attracting attention or raising suspicion.
France.

The explanation is that France had tampered with Joseph’s tobacco while he was staying at her house in Beirut. By the time he returned to Miye w Miye, the danger was already among his belongings. On Saturday evening, following his argument with Bernard, Joseph decided to stay home and smoke his argileh, completely unaware of what had happened to the tobacco beforehand.
But how did France poison the tobacco, you might wonder?

Well, let’s go back to that Spinneys receipt one last time. Remember the item listed as “Household Pest Control”? At first, it seemed like a perfectly ordinary household purchase, hardly something worth investigating. After all, products designed to eliminate unwanted household pests are commonly purchased for everyday use. But what initially appeared to be an innocent purchase turned out to be far more significant. The product, a poisonous bait designed to eliminate unwanted pests, was actually the substance France had used to contaminate Joseph’s tobacco.
And that brings us to the most important question of all: Why would France want Joseph dead?
The answer lies in the property dispute in Miye w Miye.

Throughout Joseph’s visit, Bernard had made no secret of his frustration over the property situation. He believed that Joseph should give up his claim to the house, and the disagreement had created considerable tension between them.
But Bernard wasn’t the only one who felt that way.
Remember the WhatsApp conversation between Tina and France on Saturday morning?

At first glance, the messages seemed to reinforce our suspicions about Bernard. France described her son as stubborn, expressed concern about his temper, and worried about how he might react the next time he saw Joseph.
But if you read those messages carefully, you’ll notice something else.

France herself believed that Joseph should give up the house. She argued that Bernard was the one living in Lebanon, taking care of matters in the village and managing the land, while Joseph had built his entire life in Australia. In her eyes, it made little sense for Joseph to hold on to a property he was unlikely to live in.

And when Tina reminded her that Joseph had every right to keep the house, France continued to defend Bernard’s position, insisting that giving up the property was the simplest way to put an end to the family dispute.
France wasn’t simply worried about her son’s frustration. She shared his position.

She wanted Joseph to surrender the house for Bernard’s benefit, and when it became clear that he had no intention of doing so, she began to see Joseph himself as the obstacle standing in her son’s way.
And now, let’s return to Doris for a moment.

Remember how suspicious it seemed that Doris, who was experiencing serious financial difficulties, inherited a share of Joseph’s property and sold it shortly after his death? At first, the timing made it seem as though she had a financial motive to get rid of him. But there is an important distinction between benefiting from someone’s death and deliberately causing it.

Doris did not murder Joseph to obtain an inheritance. She simply benefited financially from his death. Her financial difficulties existed before the murder, and the inheritance provided her with an unexpected opportunity to improve her situation. The fact that she sold her shares shortly afterward was suspicious, but it was not proof that she had planned Joseph’s death.
And that, ultimately, is what this entire investigation was about. Almost everyone had something that made them appear suspicious, but not every suspicious action was connected to the murder.

Perla was hiding her gambling losses and the theft of Joseph’s watch. Doris was struggling financially and benefited from an unexpected inheritance. Bernard had repeatedly argued with Joseph and possessed agricultural chemicals that made him an obvious suspect. Tina was present during Joseph’s final evening, but the evidence did not establish that she had harmed him.

And France? France appeared to be nothing more than a concerned aunt who had welcomed Joseph into her home. Her disagreement with him over an electricity bill seemed insignificant compared with the secrets everyone else was hiding.
But sometimes, the person with the least obvious secret is the one with the most to hide.
The murderer didn’t need to be the last person to see Joseph alive. The murderer didn’t need to be present at the crime scene. And the murderer didn’t need to act on the night Joseph died.
Because by the time Joseph arrived in Miye w Miye, the fatal plan had already been set in motion.
France was the reason Joseph never made it through Saturday night.
